title: A new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1–4)
word: A new heaven and a new earth
hook: God will dwell with them; no more death, mourning, crying or pain

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thousand years, read three ways, and death itself thrown away at the end. Your line was he reigns. Where did you find the big thing you share with someone? Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

Which way does heaven move? One familiar picture points up: when it's all over, people go up there. Revelation twenty-one points the other way. John sees a city, the new Jerusalem, and it's not waiting above the clouds for anyone to climb to it. It's coming down. "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." After the beasts, the fallen city, the thousand years, the closing vision of the Bible isn't people leaving earth. It's heaven arriving. Today's word is what John saw just before it: a new heaven and a new earth.

First, the opening line: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea." The prophet Isaiah had heard God promise the same thing: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth." John sees it happen. And no more sea. In chapter thirteen, the sea was where the beast rose from. Some readers hear its absence as the end of chaos and danger; others as the end of distance, nothing left to divide people. Second, God moves in. A great voice says: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God." Tabernacle is the old word for a tent, the kind Israel carried through the desert for God's presence. At the end, God pitches the tent among people. Third, what's gone. "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." Listen to the list: not a list of new things added, but of old things missing. No funerals. No hospitals. No crying in the car before you go inside. Fourth, now. Christians who read it this way say it isn't only a picture of later. It's the shape they hope toward, and some say it's why they visit the sick and sit with the grieving today: practicing a world where God lives next door.
screen: `A NEW HEAVEN, AND NO MORE SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see a world without tears. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place you know where people cry. A hospital waiting room. A courthouse hallway. A kitchen after bad news. Hold it in your mind. Now let it change, slowly. The chairs empty. No one is waiting for a call. No one is hiding red eyes. Stay with that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, you can read or say the words of Revelation twenty-one, verse four, slowly. If you don't, just let the picture rest. Then ask what one small thing would make that room a little more like it. The bell holds the time.
A new heaven and a new earth. John's vision in Revelation twenty-one: the old order passed away, God dwelling with people, and death and crying gone.
screen: `A NEW HEAVEN AND A NEW EARTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no more tears. Today, take one item from that list in hand: visit someone who is ill, or call someone who is grieving, and keep them company. Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Revelation 21:1–4 is read at Christian funerals and memorial services, and Christians speak of it as the hope behind visiting the sick, comforting the grieving and caring for the earth.

fork.setup: John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem. which way is it moving?
options: up, carrying the faithful away from earth.
down, coming from God out of heaven.
nowhere; it stays hidden behind the clouds.
fork.reveal: it comes down, "prepared as a bride adorned for her husband," and a voice says God will dwell with people. the end of the story is heaven arriving.

original.note: Greek: a tent, a dwelling. the word the King James renders tabernacle in Revelation 21:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the world, and everyone floats off to heaven.
what it means: a new heaven and earth, the holy city coming down, and God living with people, with death and crying gone.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah's promise of new heavens and a new earth, and God's tent (skene) pitched among people, as in the desert.
recall: the first and last Greek letters

notes: Two readings of 'no more sea' (end of chaos and danger; end of distance) given as 'some readers' / 'others'. Confirm.
'Tabernacle is the old word for a tent, the kind Israel carried through the desert' glosses the Greek σκηνή (tent) and links to Exodus 25:8–9; confirm wording under the claims rule.
'The usual answer points up' (hook) describes a popular assumption, not a church's teaching; confirm acceptable.
Day 1300 already used Revelation 7:17 (every tear wiped); today stresses the city coming down and God's tent, and leaves 'all things new' (21:5) for day 1312.
howItsDone says Revelation 21:1–4 is read at funerals (it appears among funeral readings in several traditions); confirm.
Editor pass: 'the usual answer' softened; 'through Revelation the sea' corrected to chapter 13; 'for Christians' limited; carry changed so it no longer repeats day 1300's tear-easing carry.
Audit 2026-10-02: SERIOUS: 'the last scene of the Bible' was wrong (21:2 is not the last scene; ch 22 follows); now 'the closing vision'.
